scale.label: Ad hoc
scale.note: Nothing is defined; things get handled when there is time.

scale.label: Reactive
scale.note: Basic rules exist, but they are applied only once a problem appears.

scale.label: Proactive
scale.note: The policy is written and shared, reviews take place and some of it is automated.

scale.label: Optimised
scale.note: Fully automated, measurable and continuously improved.

areas.title: Vision, strategy and governance leadership
areas.why: Without a vision and a steering team, a governance plan falls apart into isolated IT settings. This section asks whether a strategic framework exists and who decides about SharePoint Online.

questions.text: Is there a written vision or strategy for SharePoint Online?

levels.L0: No vision exists; SPO came with Microsoft 365 and is used ad hoc.
levels.L1: IT has an informal idea, but it is neither written down nor shared.
levels.L2: The vision is written, approved by a sponsor and shared with key stakeholders.
levels.L3: The vision is published on the governance site, tied to the company digital workplace strategy and reviewed regularly.

questions.text: Is there a working steering or governance committee for Microsoft 365 and SPO?

levels.L0: No steering committee.
levels.L1: Occasional ad hoc meetings between IT and one or two people from the business.
levels.L2: A formal committee (IT + business + security/compliance) that meets regularly, at least quarterly.
levels.L3: A committee with a clear charter, agenda, decision rights, an escalation path to top management and documented decisions.

questions.text: Are decision rights clear — who decides and how are conflicts escalated?

levels.L0: Whoever shouts loudest decides.
levels.L1: IT decides, but without a formal mandate.
levels.L2: Decision rights for typical situations are defined (who approves exceptions, who approves new features).
levels.L3: A full RACI matrix for decisions, an escalation path and documentation of key decisions.

areas.title: Roles and responsibilities
areas.why: When nobody is accountable, sites end up without an owner, permissions creep and content goes stale.

questions.text: Do site owners have clearly defined responsibilities?

levels.L0: Site owner is a technical term; nobody knows what the role involves.
levels.L1: Owners are assigned, but their responsibilities are not written down anywhere.
levels.L2: A document describing what a site owner does (permissions, sharing, retention, attestation) exists and is shared.
levels.L3: Responsibilities are part of the job description or onboarding pack, with mandatory training before the role is granted.

questions.text: Is there a RACI matrix for the key processes (provisioning, sharing, retention, incidents)?

levels.L0: No RACI; everything is ad hoc.
levels.L1: A RACI for one or two processes, mostly informal.
levels.L2: The RACI covers the main processes (provisioning, permissions, sharing, retention).
levels.L3: A RACI for all key processes, reviewed regularly and tied to the governance plan.

questions.text: How many tenant-level administrators (Global Admin, SharePoint Admin) do you have, and do you apply least privilege?

levels.L0: Most of the IT team holds Global Admin, with no separation.
levels.L1: There are several administrators, but the roles are not separated (SP Admin, Compliance Admin and so on).
levels.L2: Roles are separated by responsibility and the number of holders is limited.
levels.L3: Privileged Identity Management with just-in-time access, at most two to four Global Admin accounts and regular access reviews.

areas.title: Policies, standards and guidelines
areas.why: A policy is a binding rule, a guideline a recommendation. Without the distinction — and without publishing them — users get lost in the rules.

questions.text: Is there a consolidated governance plan, published where users can find it?

levels.L0: No governance plan exists, or it is a PDF in somebody folder.
levels.L1: The plan exists, but in a document the user has to go looking for.
levels.L2: The plan is published on a governance SharePoint site and linked from the relevant places.
levels.L3: The governance site carries the plan plus training materials, an FAQ and a way to give feedback, with navigation integrated into the intranet.

questions.text: Do you have naming conventions for sites, Microsoft 365 groups, teams and files?

levels.L0: No conventions; everyone names things their own way.
levels.L1: Recommendations exist, but nothing is technically enforced.
levels.L2: The Microsoft 365 group naming policy is active (prefix, suffix, blocked words) and site rules are documented.
levels.L3: Fully enforced technically (Entra naming policy, custom provisioning workflow), with file rules in the authoring guidance.

questions.text: Is there a process for exceptions to the policies?

levels.L0: Exceptions are not handled; things simply get done.
levels.L1: Exceptions are agreed ad hoc and never recorded.
levels.L2: An exception process (form, approver, register) is defined.
levels.L3: Exceptions are recorded with an expiry date and an owner, reviewed regularly and visible on a dashboard.

areas.title: Information architecture
areas.why: Without a sound information architecture users cannot find anything, search fails and Copilot returns nonsense.

questions.text: Do you have a defined global navigation (app bar) and a home site?

levels.L0: No home site, the default app bar and chaotic navigation.
levels.L1: A home site exists, but it is not connected to the navigation.
levels.L2: A designed home site plus an app bar configured with global links.
levels.L3: App bar, home site, Viva Connections and audience targeting in the navigation.

questions.text: Do you have a strategy for hub sites (HR, finance, IT, business units, projects and so on)?

levels.L0: No hub sites, just flat site collections.
levels.L1: One or two hubs created, but without consistency.
levels.L2: Hub sites for the key areas, with hub owners and rules for associating sites.
levels.L3: Multi-level hub-to-hub association, hub-scoped search and a hub design system.

questions.text: Do you use a taxonomy and managed metadata (term store, content types)?

levels.L0: Folders only, no metadata.
levels.L1: Free-text columns, used locally only.
levels.L2: A term store with organisationally approved terms and content types for the main kinds of content.
levels.L3: An enterprise content type hub, automatic population (Syntex) and refiners in search.

areas.title: Provisioning and site lifecycle
areas.why: Uncontrolled creation and forgotten sites are the biggest source of content sprawl and security risk.

questions.text: How does a new SharePoint site or Microsoft 365 group or team come into being?

levels.L0: Anyone can create one, at any time, with no process.
levels.L1: Self-service is enabled, with no approval and no metadata.
levels.L2: Self-service with a form (Power Automate or Forms), an approver and automatic assignment of owner and category.
levels.L3: A fully automated workflow, integration with ITSM, site templates by purpose and post-provisioning attestation.

questions.text: Do you have the Microsoft 365 groups expiration policy switched on?

levels.L0: Not switched on; no group ever expires.
levels.L1: Switched on with a very long horizon (for example 730 days) and no follow-up.
levels.L2: Switched on with a sensible horizon (180 to 365 days), notifications work and auto-renewal follows activity.
levels.L3: Switched on per segment (sensitive groups have a shorter life), with automatic escalation and reporting.

questions.text: Do you use SharePoint Advanced Management site lifecycle policies (inactive site, ownership, attestation)?

levels.L0: We do not have SAM, or no policies are configured.
levels.L1: We have SAM, but only ad hoc reports and no active policies.
levels.L2: An active inactive-site policy plus an ownership policy in simulation or active mode.
levels.L3: The full set of policies (inactive, ownership, attestation) in active mode, with automatic actions and a dashboard.

questions.text: Do you have a defined process for archiving and decommissioning sites?

levels.L0: Sites are never deleted, only added.
levels.L1: Something gets deleted occasionally; there is no formal process.
levels.L2: A defined process (who approves, how it is backed up, how users are notified).
levels.L3: Microsoft 365 Archive deployed, integration with legal hold and reporting over archived sites.

areas.title: Content management
areas.why: Poor content management means broken search, duplicates and out-of-date information feeding Copilot.

questions.text: Do users have clear rules about where to store what (OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams chat, e-mail)?

levels.L0: No rules; everyone stores things wherever they like.
levels.L1: A general recommendation exists, but it is not shared.
levels.L2: The rules are part of the governance materials and training, and users know them.
levels.L3: The rules are backed by automatic classification and guidance in Copilot (for example, this file belongs in a Teams channel).

questions.text: Do you use content types and structured metadata in libraries?

levels.L0: Libraries use folders only, with no metadata.
levels.L1: A few custom columns here and there, without consistency.
levels.L2: Centrally managed content types for the key kinds of content (contracts, invoices, project documents).
levels.L3: An enterprise content type hub, automatic population through Syntex or Power Automate and refiners in search.

questions.text: Do you have a versioning policy configured in your libraries?

levels.L0: Default settings; nobody looks after it.
levels.L1: The default of 500 versions, with some libraries lowered to risky values.
levels.L2: Versioning is set deliberately per kind of library and documented.
levels.L3: Versioning plus content approval and check-out where it makes sense, with monitoring.

areas.title: Security, identity and permissions
areas.why: Permissions tend to creep. Broken inheritance, Everyone-except-external-users and direct sharing add up to an attack surface that Copilot makes visible.

questions.text: Are permissions managed exclusively through groups (Microsoft Entra security groups, Microsoft 365 groups), or assigned directly to users?

levels.L0: Most permissions are assigned directly to users.
levels.L1: A mix of direct assignments and groups, with no formal rule.
levels.L2: A groups-only policy, with occasional exceptions.
levels.L3: Strictly through groups (security or Microsoft 365), validated by site access reviews and enforced technically.

questions.text: Do you know which sites have broken permission inheritance, Everyone-except-external-users sharing and Anyone links?

levels.L0: We have no idea how many such sites there are.
levels.L1: We suspect it is a problem, but we have no numbers.
levels.L2: We generate data access governance reports regularly (SAM) and know the numbers.
levels.L3: Data access governance reports plus automatic alerts, a remediation workflow and site access reviews.

questions.text: Do you have conditional access policies for SharePoint Online?

levels.L0: No conditional access policies for SPO.
levels.L1: Basic multifactor authentication, but nothing specific to SPO.
levels.L2: Conditional access for SPO (multifactor, device compliance, location) with session controls.
levels.L3: Advanced conditional access (sign-in risk, app protection, restricted access control for sensitive sites), reviewed regularly.

questions.text: Do site access reviews take place regularly?

levels.L0: No access reviews.
levels.L1: Occasional ad hoc checks during audits.
levels.L2: Scheduled access reviews delegated to site owners (Entra ID Governance or SAM).
levels.L3: Automated on a cycle, escalated when not completed and integrated with offboarding.

areas.title: External sharing and B2B collaboration
areas.why: External sharing is the most visible risk and the most frequent business request. The goal is not to forbid it but to aim it.

questions.text: What is the tenant-level external sharing setting in SPO?

levels.L0: Anyone (anonymous links), with no expiry.
levels.L1: Anyone, but with an expiry.
levels.L2: New and existing guests (B2B through Entra), with no anonymous links for sensitive data.
levels.L3: Differentiated per site (existing guests for sensitive sites, new and existing for ordinary ones), with a strict default at site level.

questions.text: What is the default sharing link type, and is it limited?

levels.L0: The default is Anyone with the link, can edit, with no expiry.
levels.L1: Anyone, view only, with no expiry.
levels.L2: The default is People with existing access or Specific people, with anonymous links expiring in 30 to 90 days.
levels.L3: A per-site override for the intranet (existing access) versus project sites (specific people), with restrictive defaults.

questions.text: Do you limit sharing by domain or by security group?

levels.L0: No limits; anyone can share with anyone.
levels.L1: Only problematic domains are blocked, ad hoc.
levels.L2: An allowlist of partner domains plus a security group limiting who may share externally.
levels.L3: Cross-tenant access settings in Entra, granular control per organisation and a regularly reviewed allowlist.

questions.text: Do guests (B2B) expire automatically?

levels.L0: Guests stay in the tenant forever.
levels.L1: Occasional manual clean-up.
levels.L2: A guest expiration policy is switched on (for example 60 to 180 days), with reauthentication through a verification code.
levels.L3: The full Entra ID Governance access lifecycle, access packages and periodic access reviews for guests.

areas.title: Information protection, compliance and retention
areas.why: GDPR, NIS2 and sector regulation all touch the data in SPO. Without retention you either delete what you must keep, or keep everything forever.

questions.text: Do you have a defined data classification (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted)?

levels.L0: No classification.
levels.L1: A classification exists on paper but is not applied.
levels.L2: The classification is in place, with sensitivity labels defined and published.
levels.L3: Classification plus auto-labeling (trainable classifiers) and container labels on sites and Microsoft 365 groups.

questions.text: How deeply are sensitivity labels deployed in SPO and OneDrive?

levels.L0: We do not use them.
levels.L1: Labels exist, but users do not apply them.
levels.L2: Manual labeling is in use, with default labels on selected libraries.
levels.L3: Auto-labeling policies for sensitive information types, container labels and integration with DLP and Copilot.

questions.text: Do you have retention policies for SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams?

levels.L0: No retention policies.
levels.L1: Only a basic one (for example retention across the whole tenant for a number of years).
levels.L2: Differentiated policies (per location, per kind of content) with retention labels for the exceptions.
levels.L3: The full Purview Data Lifecycle Management framework, records management for high-value content and disposition review.

questions.text: Do you have active data loss prevention policies for SPO and OneDrive, and for Copilot?

levels.L0: No DLP.
levels.L1: A DLP pilot for one or two information types (for example card numbers).
levels.L2: DLP policies for the main sensitive types (personal data, finance, intellectual property) with policy tips for users.
levels.L3: A full DLP framework plus DLP for Copilot, integration with Insider Risk Management and adaptive protection.

questions.text: Are you ready for eDiscovery and audit (legal hold, search, export)?

levels.L0: We have never done it and do not know how.
levels.L1: eDiscovery Standard, with an informal procedure.
levels.L2: eDiscovery Premium deployed, audit log retention of a year or more and a documented process.
levels.L3: Regular drills, integration with the legal team and audit log retention into a SIEM.

areas.title: Search and findability
areas.why: Search is the main gateway to content and the raw material for Copilot. What search cannot find, Copilot cannot use.

questions.text: Is Microsoft Search deliberately configured (start page, scopes, verticals)?

levels.L0: Default settings, nothing adjusted.
levels.L1: A few small tweaks, with no strategy.
levels.L2: Search verticals, result types and scopes defined per persona or hub.
levels.L3: A fully curated search experience, audience targeting and Graph connectors for non-Microsoft systems.

questions.text: Do you manage promoted results, bookmarks, acronyms and Q&A?

levels.L0: We do not use them.
levels.L1: A few bookmarks, ad hoc.
levels.L2: Bookmarks, acronyms and Q&A for the typical queries, maintained regularly.
levels.L3: A named owner and a dashboard, with integration of helpdesk data (frequent questions become bookmarks).

questions.text: Do you watch search analytics (top queries, queries with no result) and use them to improve?

levels.L0: We do not watch them.
levels.L1: An occasional look at the default reports.
levels.L2: Regular review; the top no-result queries lead to new bookmarks or content.
levels.L3: Search analytics feed the information architecture roadmap, with a KPI for search success rate.

areas.title: User experience, branding and accessibility
areas.why: A consistent look builds trust and lowers cognitive load. Accessibility is often a legal obligation.

questions.text: Are consistent brand standards applied to the intranet and SharePoint sites?

levels.L0: The default theme, no branding.
levels.L1: A custom theme applied here and there, without consistency.
levels.L2: Brand standards defined, a theme plus an organisation assets library (logos, photos), applied to the key sites.
levels.L3: A design system plus site templates, Viva Connections branding and multilingual support.

questions.text: Do you use site templates or site designs to standardise new sites?

levels.L0: We do not; every site is built from scratch.
levels.L1: A few templates, ad hoc.
levels.L2: A set of templates for the typical scenarios (department, project, external collaboration).
levels.L3: Templates with a lifecycle (proposal, active, knowledge capture, archive) and automation through Power Automate.

questions.text: Do you test the accessibility (WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 AA) of intranet pages and templates?

levels.L0: We do not test and do not know where we stand.
levels.L1: An occasional check, visual only.
levels.L2: Authors have guidance and the accessibility checker is used before publishing.
levels.L3: A regular accessibility audit (internal or external), reporting and mandatory fixes before publishing.

questions.text: Do you support multilingual content (multi-language pages, a translation workflow)?

levels.L0: One language only; not needed.
levels.L1: Manual translations, handled differently on each site.
levels.L2: Multi-language pages (modern SPO) with a translation workflow.
levels.L3: A full framework plus audience targeting by language and integration with a translation service.

areas.title: Customisation, development and Power Platform
areas.why: Customisation unlocks value, but without governance the Power Platform becomes shadow IT.

questions.text: Is there a customisation policy (what is allowed: configuration, branding, no-code, SPFx, pro-code)?

levels.L0: No policy; anyone can do anything.
levels.L1: Informal rules inside IT.
levels.L2: A written policy with an approval process for SPFx and the app catalog.
levels.L3: Full application lifecycle management (dev, test, production), code review, dependency scanning and deployment monitoring.

questions.text: Do you govern the Power Platform (environments, DLP policies, maker roles)?

levels.L0: The default environment is the wild west, with no DLP.
levels.L1: A few dedicated environments, but no DLP.
levels.L2: An environment strategy (dev, test, production, dedicated ones for SharePoint forms) with DLP policies defined.
levels.L3: A Power Platform centre of excellence, the CoE Starter Kit, monitoring and a citizen developer programme.

questions.text: Do you know which non-Microsoft applications reach SPO content?

levels.L0: We have no overview.
levels.L1: An occasional look at Entra enterprise applications.
levels.L2: App insights reports (SAM) and restricted site creation by apps.
levels.L3: A full app governance programme, approval of new applications, monitoring and alerting.

areas.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot and agent governance
areas.why: Copilot exposes everything that relied on security through obscurity. Without preparation you get either a blocked rollout or an incident.

questions.text: Have you run a Copilot readiness assessment (Content Management Assessment in SAM, or a DSPM data risk assessment in Purview)?

levels.L0: We have not.
levels.L1: A pilot assessment, but no action taken.
levels.L2: The assessment was done and the high-risk sites it identified were remediated.
levels.L3: A regular (quarterly) assessment with a dashboard and continuous remediation.

questions.text: Do you use Restricted Content Discovery or Restricted SharePoint Search for sensitive sites?

levels.L0: We do not; everything is in Copilot grounding.
levels.L1: A few sites marked by hand, without a system.
levels.L2: The identified high-risk sites have Restricted Content Discovery active, with a documented process.
levels.L3: A strict strategy (Restricted SharePoint Search allowlist) or a protect strategy (Restricted Content Discovery by risk), reviewed regularly.

questions.text: Do you govern SharePoint agents (who may build them, on what data, with what monitoring)?

levels.L0: We do not; agents appear without control.
levels.L1: IT knows about them but has no tool to monitor them.
levels.L2: The agent insights report (SAM) is reviewed regularly and sensitivity labels are respected.
levels.L3: A full agent lifecycle, approval for company-wide agents, cost monitoring and a Purview audit.

areas.title: Monitoring, audit and reporting
areas.why: What is not measured is not managed. Without an audit trail you can neither investigate an incident nor prove compliance.

questions.text: How regularly do you review the native admin reports (SharePoint admin center, Microsoft 365 usage)?

levels.L0: Never.
levels.L1: Somebody takes a look when there is a problem.
levels.L2: A monthly review with a named owner.
levels.L3: Automated reporting into Power BI or Sentinel, with a dashboard for stakeholders.

questions.text: Do you use the SAM data access governance reports (sharing links, permissions, Everyone-except-external-users, sensitivity labels)?

levels.L0: We do not have SAM, or we do not use it.
levels.L1: An occasional ad hoc run of a report.
levels.L2: Regular reporting; AI insights generate recommendations and the actions get done.
levels.L3: Automated through PowerShell, integrated with a remediation workflow and tracked as a KPI.

questions.text: Do you send audit logs (Purview Audit) to a SIEM such as Sentinel, or to another security tool?

levels.L0: Audit logs stay in Purview with basic retention only.
levels.L1: An occasional export for an audit.
levels.L2: Audit log retention of a year or more, with alert policies for the key events.
levels.L3: Streaming into Sentinel or another SIEM, correlated with other Microsoft 365 and Defender signals, with hunt queries.

questions.text: Do you have a governance KPI dashboard (in Power BI or directly in Microsoft 365)?

levels.L0: No dashboard.
levels.L1: Occasional Excel reports for management.
levels.L2: A regular dashboard with KPIs (permissions, sharing, lifecycle, adoption).
levels.L3: A real-time dashboard for IT and executives, with drill-down and benchmarking.

areas.title: Backup, recovery and business continuity
areas.why: Microsoft protects the platform, not losses caused by users. A 93-day recycle bin is not enough for most compliance scenarios.

questions.text: What backup strategy do you have for SPO, OneDrive and Teams?

levels.L0: We rely on the recycle bin alone, with no further backup.
levels.L1: The recycle bin plus user awareness of versioning.
levels.L2: Microsoft 365 Backup or a third-party backup (Veeam, AvePoint, Rubrik) with retention set by compliance.
levels.L3: A layered strategy (Microsoft 365 Backup plus third-party plus offsite), tested regularly.

questions.text: Do you have a defined recovery point objective and recovery time objective?

levels.L0: We do not.
levels.L1: We have a sense of how fast, but only informally.
levels.L2: RPO and RTO defined per data classification and documented.
levels.L3: Measured, tested, validated and backed by an SLA with the business owners.

questions.text: Do you run regular disaster recovery tests?

levels.L0: Never.
levels.L1: A one-off test when the backup solution was introduced.
levels.L2: An annual test with the results and lessons documented.
levels.L3: A test plan per scenario (mass delete, compromised account, regional outage), run regularly and integrated with incident response.

questions.text: Do you have a defined process for the OneDrive of a departing employee?

levels.L0: It either stays forever or gets deleted at random.
levels.L1: IT handles it by hand when a manager asks.
levels.L2: A defined offboarding workflow with a retention period and delegation to the manager.
levels.L3: An automated workflow through Entra ID lifecycle workflows, integrated with the HR system and audited.

areas.title: Adoption, training and support
areas.why: Without adoption the best governance plan is worthless. Adoption is the last mile of governance.

questions.text: Do you have an adoption strategy with defined scenarios and success criteria?

levels.L0: No strategy, just a rollout.
levels.L1: A communication campaign at launch, and nothing afterwards.
levels.L2: A strategy with scenarios per persona, a communication plan and training.
levels.L3: A full change management framework (Prosci or ADKAR), executive sponsorship and a long-term campaign.

questions.text: Is there a champions network (ambassadors inside the business)?

levels.L0: No; IT is on its own.
levels.L1: A few enthusiasts, unstructured.
levels.L2: A formal champions programme with regular meetings and recognition.
levels.L3: A fully structured programme with a defined role, KPIs, mentoring and a place in training for newcomers.

questions.text: Is there regular training for site owners?

levels.L0: No training.
levels.L1: Occasional ad hoc workshops.
levels.L2: Mandatory onboarding for new site owners (permissions, sharing, retention basics).
levels.L3: A structured course with certification, refreshed annually and tied to the role in Entra.

questions.text: Do you measure adoption metrics and use them to iterate?

levels.L0: We do not track them.
levels.L1: An occasional look at the Microsoft 365 adoption score.
levels.L2: Regular reporting (monthly active users, content engagement, search success) plus feedback from champions.
levels.L3: A full adoption dashboard, net promoter score, correlation with business metrics and a quarterly review.

areas.title: Migration and platform evolution
areas.why: A migration is an opportunity — and a necessity — to reset governance. The platform keeps evolving and the governance plan has to keep up.

questions.text: Do you still have file shares, on-premises SharePoint or other systems to migrate into SPO?

levels.L0: Yes, a lot of them, with no migration plan.
levels.L1: Yes, some, with a vague idea of migrating.
levels.L2: Migration runs in planned waves and governance is settled beforehand.
levels.L3: Almost everything is in Microsoft 365, the rest has a planned sunset and hybrid governance is resolved.

questions.text: Does anybody actively follow the Microsoft 365 roadmap and message center?

levels.L0: Nobody.
levels.L1: IT reacts to breaking changes from time to time.
levels.L2: A named owner, a monthly review and communication with the area owners.
levels.L3: An innovation backlog, evaluation of new features and a pilot programme through targeted release.

questions.text: Is the tenant, or a selected group of users, on targeted release to pilot new features?

levels.L0: Standard release, no pilot.
levels.L1: We know it exists but do not use it.
levels.L2: Targeted release for IT and champions, with a formal pilot process.
levels.L3: Full release management with validation and a communication plan for every new feature.

areas.title: Measurement, KPIs and continuous improvement
areas.why: KPIs make the case for investment, prove value and reveal where the governance plan and reality have parted ways.

questions.text: Do you have a defined set of governance KPIs (health, adoption, compliance, value)?

levels.L0: No KPIs.
levels.L1: A few metrics, ad hoc.
levels.L2: A defined set of KPIs (governance health, adoption, compliance), measured regularly.
levels.L3: KPIs integrated with business metrics, an executive dashboard and targets set each quarter.

questions.text: Does a quarterly governance review take place (committee, KPIs, roadmap)?

levels.L0: No.
levels.L1: Occasional informal meetings.
levels.L2: A regular quarterly meeting with an agenda, action items and follow-up.
levels.L3: A formal quarterly business review with executive stakeholders, documentation and public commitments.

questions.text: Do you have an active user feedback loop (surveys, focus groups, site owner sentiment)?

levels.L0: No feedback loop.
levels.L1: An occasional survey.
levels.L2: A regular net promoter score or pulse survey, feedback from champions and action on the results.
levels.L3: Continuous feedback (Viva Pulse, Forms Pro), correlated with adoption data and a transparent action plan.
